_about: Spoken scripts for the Word Detectives story pages (voice: Higgsfield preset Gracie, id 09878754-f20b-5330-9790-58a8027ab5b2, model seed_audio, mp3). Keys are <levelId>-<pageIndex>. Letters and old spellings are written out so a TTS voice says them correctly. Recorded clips go in public/story/<key>.mp3.
freeze-0: English is very old. English is more than one thousand years old. Long ago, people spelt words just the way they said them. In the word knight, every letter was spoken, even the K.
freeze-1: Then came the printing press. In fourteen seventy-six, William Caxton set up the first printing press in England. Once a word had been printed in thousands of books, everyone copied that spelling. Spelling began to freeze.
freeze-2: But talking kept changing. People went on changing the way they spoke. Some sounds faded away, and others shifted. The spelling stayed where it was.
freeze-3: Spellings are fossils. So a strange spelling is often a fossil. It shows how the word sounded hundreds of years ago. Word detectives read those clues.
cute-0: Cut, and cute. Add the letter E to cut, and you get cute. The letter U now says its own name. But why put an E there, if we never say it?
cute-1: The E used to be spoken. Hundreds of years ago, lots of words ended in a little 'uh' sound. Name was said, nah-muh. Time was said, tee-muh. That is why they were written with an E.
cute-2: The sound left, the job stayed. Slowly, people stopped saying the 'uh'. But the E was still useful. It told readers that the vowel before it was long.
cute-3: So writers kept using it. The silent E became a signal. Writers used it for newer words too, like cute. It is not magic. It is a leftover sound that found a new job.
busy-e-0: Job one: make the vowel long. This is the one you know. Hop becomes hope. Cub becomes cube. Cut becomes cute.
busy-e-1: Job two: guard the letter V. English words do not like to end in the letter V. So an E stands guard after it. That is why have, give, and love end in E, even though the vowel is short.
busy-e-2: Job three: soften C and G. Before an E, the letter C makes a sss sound, and the letter G makes a juh sound. Take the E off dance, or large, and they would end in hard sounds.
busy-e-3: Job four: I am not a plural. The letter S on the end usually means more than one. The E shows that the S belongs to the word. Tens, spelt T, E, N, S, means lots of ten. Tense, spelt T, E, N, S, E, is a different word.
gh-0: A sound English lost. The letters G H used to stand for a rough sound made at the back of the mouth, like the end of the Scottish word loch. Night sounded like nicht. German still says Nacht for night, and Licht for light.
gh-1: The sound faded away. Over time, people stopped making that sound. In night, light, high, eight, and daughter, it went completely silent. The letters stayed, as a fossil.
gh-2: Sometimes it turned into F. In a few words, the rough sound did not vanish. It changed into a fff sound. That is why laugh, cough, enough, rough, and tough all end with a fff sound.
gh-3: And what about ghost? Ghost used to be spelt G, O, S, T. It is thought that Caxton's printers, who came from Flanders, added the H, because their own word was spelt G, H, E, E, S, T. At the start of a word, G H always makes a hard guh sound.
quiet-0: Kuh-nee, and kuh-night. The K in knee, knot, knife, and know used to be spoken. Try saying kuh, nnn, quickly. It is hard work! Over time, people dropped the K. German still says the K in its word for knee: kuh-nee.
quiet-1: Write, and gnaw. The same thing happened to the W in write, wrong, and wrist, and to the G in gnaw and gnat. Each one was once a real sound.
quiet-2: Lamb, and comb. The letter B at the end of lamb, comb, and climb was spoken too. After the letter M, it slowly melted away.
quiet-3: Why keep them? Because they help your eyes. A silent letter tells apart words that sound the same. A knight in armour is not the night time. And to write with a pen is not the same as being right.
scholars-0: The scholars who loved Latin. About five hundred years ago, many scholars thought Latin was the finest language. They wanted English words to show off their Latin roots.
scholars-1: So they added letters. Debt was spelt D, E, T, T, E. Scholars added a B, to match the Latin word, debitum. Doubt was spelt D, O, U, T, E. They added a B there too, to match the Latin word, dubitare. Receipt gained a P, and salmon gained an L.
scholars-2: Nobody ever said them. These letters are different from the K in knee. They were never spoken in English at all. They were added only on paper.
scholars-3: The island mistake. Island was once spelt I, L, A, N, D. Scholars thought it came from the Latin word insula, like the word isle, so they added an S. They were wrong! It was an old English word all along. The S stayed anyway.
family-0: Spelling shows family. English spelling does two jobs. It shows how a word sounds, and it shows which words belong together. Words from the same family keep the same letters, even when the sound changes.
family-1: Sign, and signal. Sign has a silent G. But listen to signal, and signature. There is the G, loud and clear! The silent G in sign shows they are relatives.
family-2: Two, and twin. Why is there a W in the number two? Because two belongs with twin, twice, twelve, and twenty. You can hear the W in all of those.
family-3: A detective trick. When you cannot remember a silent letter, look for a relative where you can hear it. Muscle is hard to spell, until you think of muscular.
love-0: Books written by hand. Before printing, every book was copied by hand with a quill. The letters U, N, M, V, and W were all made from the same short straight strokes.
love-1: A row of sticks. Put those letters side by side, and a word turned into a row of sticks. Love, spelt L, U, V, or monk, spelt M, U, N, K, was very hard to read. Which strokes were the U?
love-2: The clever fix. Many experts think the writers solved it by changing the U to an O next to those letters. A round O is easy to spot among the sticks.
love-3: So O says 'uh'. That is why love, come, some, son, monk, and wonder are written with an O, but said with the 'uh' sound in cup.
borrowed-0: English is a collector. English has borrowed words from languages all over the world. Often it kept the spelling from the word's first home. That is why one letter pair can have different sounds.
borrowed-1: Clues from Greek. In words from Greek, C H makes a kuh sound, as in school. And P H makes a fff sound, as in photo.
borrowed-2: Clues from French. In words from French, C H makes a shh sound, as in chef. Q, U, E on the end makes a kuh sound, as in unique. And a T on the end can be silent, as in ballet.
borrowed-3: Clues from Italian. Italian gave us food and music words. Its double Z makes a tss sound, as in pizza. And G H keeps a G hard, as in spaghetti.
ie-ei-0: The rule with a secret. I before E, except after C, seems to fail all the time. The secret is that it only works when the letters make a long E sound, as in see.
ie-ei-1: Step one: the long E sound. If you hear a long E, as in field, write I, then E.
ie-ei-2: Step two: long E after C. If you hear a long E straight after the letter C, write E, then I. Receive, deceive, and perceive are one family. They all come from a Latin word that means, to take.
ie-ei-3: Step three: the A sound. If you hear the sound A, as in eight, write E, then I.
ie-ei-4: The rule-breakers. A few words break the rule, and just have to be learnt. The best one to remember is weird, because it is weird.
